Inset text, focus cues and targets from rounded boundaries; preserve every action in effective working area at supported real scales.

motionAndFeedback.sourceScope: The supplied library uses Windows Runtime XAML controls, dependency properties and storyboards. Transfer its interaction principles to the existing PowerShell/.NET Framework WinForms host; XAML theme APIs are not a drop-in implementation. The Win32 animation UX guide is legacy Windows7 guidance used only for supporting accessibility/performance principles.
motionAndFeedback.current: OutlineButton paints immediate hover, pressed and keyboard-focus feedback; StatusBadge paints state colors. No animation scheduler or motion recipe is present. Apply runs synchronous work after refreshing progress text. A UI-thread animation timer would pause during that work.
motionAndFeedback.decision: Keep immediate native feedback as the first implementation. Prioritize explicit selection/operation state, busy guarding and the existing geometry fixes. Optional paint-only motion can be evaluated afterward; it is not a release requirement or a gameplay change.

proposedRecipe.trialScope: HRS starting point for a future reviewed experiment, not a Microsoft-mandated duration. Interpolate background/accent paint only; new state text, accessibility information, focus and action gates update immediately. Avoid fading essential text.
proposedRecipe.reducedMotion: Respect system client-area animation preference; disabled or unavailable preference means instant rendering.
proposedRecipe.highContrast: Immediate system-color rendering; omit decorative interpolation.

hostAdapter: If optional effects are implemented, query SystemParametersInfoW with SPI_GETCLIENTAREAANIMATION (0x1042), uiParam=0, a marshalled Win32 BOOL output and fWinIni=0. Check the API return value; query failure falls back to instant rendering.
Read the preference before effects and refresh when Windows settings change. The manager must not set global Windows animation preferences.

Keep effect scheduling bounded and on the UI thread; use elapsed time rather than assumed tick counts. A newer state replaces the prior effect and snaps or retargets to the current state. Disabled/disposed controls and a closed manager cancel pending effects; stop and dispose any timers when idle or closed.

Generate the implementation from the upstream native controls/design recipe and update provenance hashes. Those upstream generator inputs are absent in this QA transfer. Do not add XAML dependencies or ship another source-string override for motion.
operationContract: Applying feedback begins only when the confirmed write operation starts. Use readable Applying settings... text and an explicit guard against conflicting/repeated commands. Static feedback is valid when animations are disabled.

Animated progress never estimates completion from elapsed time. Report numeric progress only from measured stages; do not add sleeps, artificial delays or nested DoEvents pumping to make effects visible.

Verified installation/readback, matching policy and required confirmation acknowledgement remain the authority for Applied/Launch readiness. Neither an effect ending nor a screenshot of green status establishes successful Apply.

The trader-assignment warning remains readable in the Settings Applied acknowledgement dialog until acknowledged. Motion must not shorten its visibility, auto-dismiss it or substitute for acknowledgement.

Cancelling a visual effect does not cancel an install transaction. Preserve automatic failed-Apply byte recovery. Measure blocking duration before proposing worker-thread changes; a spinner alone cannot make synchronous UI work responsive.
Keep window bounds, row heights, scroll extent and hit targets stable during feedback. Do not animate fit/resize operations while the existing width, work-area and scrolling defects remain open.
tooling: Extend the future recipe validator with allowed effect names, bounded finite durations and mandatory instant fallback. Keep motion settings separate from gameplay policy and operational state.

Add harmless preview fixtures for Normal/Hover/Pressed/Focused/Disabled and Pending/Applying/Applied/Blocked states, with install, launch and uninstall callbacks neutralized. Label their screenshots as simulated presentation evidence.

Record candidate/recipe/control hashes, actual display scale, High Contrast, effective animation preference, selected effect/duration, state identifier, timestamps and fixture/live scope alongside captures.

For optional motion, inspect initial, sampled intermediate and settled frames plus rapid state changes. Still images verify appearance; brief human observation or a recording is needed to judge flicker and smoothness.

Automation should wait for explicit state and a bounded rendering-settled condition, not fixed sleeps or animation completion as an operation result. Capture a timeout as failure; retain live transaction/readback evidence separately.
acceptance: Windows animations on/off and preference-query failure produce the same final text, enabled actions and policy; the off/failure paths show the state immediately.
Mouse and keyboard receive immediate pressed/focus feedback; disabled controls never appear pressed or accept actions.
Rapid input, a new status, disabling a control and closing the window leave no stale effect, idle timer or disposed-control callback.
High Contrast and actual supported display scales retain readable text, focus and reachable controls at normal/minimum sizes and on the secondary monitor.
Selection and visual fixture exercises perform no disk writes, game launches or uninstall operations.
Busy rendering does not permit duplicate/conflicting writes; failure shows the correct state and preserves the existing automatic recovery contract.
Real Apply qualification verifies readback and acknowledgement before Launch; visual fixtures never count as that operational pass.
Effects add no required wait, moving hit target, window-size drift or flashing. If the optional effect is distracting or stutters in the actual host, retain instant rendering.
